cases.prompt: Compare the conservation approaches for the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes.

response.response_text:
Both the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes share a foundation of intensive human intervention to pull critically endangered flightless birds back from the brink — but they differ in their habitats, specific techniques, and the directions they're now heading. Both programmes are managed by the Department of Conservation (DOC) and represent some of New Zealand's most ambitious and resource-heavy conservation efforts.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Shared Foundation: Predator-Free Islands and Intensive Management

The most fundamental strategy common to both programmes is the relocation of birds to predator-free island sanctuaries. For kākāpō, all 61 surviving Stewart Island birds were transferred between 1982 and 1992 to safe havens including Whenua Hou/Codfish Island, Te Hoiere/Maud Island, and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island, after feral cats had halved the population in just five years. [[1]](cite://1/1) The only safe place for kākāpō to breed is on these predator-free islands, where even then, workers install infrared movement sensors and surveillance cameras at every nest. [[2]](cite://2/1)

For takahē, a similar strategy was employed — "security populations" were established on predator-free offshore islands, and a Specially Protected Area was created in the Murchison Mountains to protect the remaining wild population. [[3]](cite://3/1) Takahē are also bred in semi-captivity at the Burwood Takahē Centre near Te Anau, within predator-proof pens. [[4]](cite://4/1)

## Kākāpō: Hyper-Intensive, Technology-Driven Management

The kākāpō programme has been characterised by an extraordinary level of hands-on intervention. During breeding seasons, over 100 volunteer nest minders from around the world have participated in 24-hour surveillance of nests, acting as surrogate parents while females forage at night. [[5]](cite://5/1) The primary goal of all this activity has been to increase the survival rate of eggs and chicks by identifying problems early, keeping eggs and chicks warm during the female's absences, reducing infection risk, and hand-rearing any chicks in trouble. [[6]](cite://6/1)

Innovative technology has been central to the kākāpō effort. Scientist Graeme Elliott developed a "boom box" — a portable weatherproof stereo system placed near leks to play back male booming calls and encourage courtship — and even experimented with injecting rimu trees with hormones to stimulate fruiting, since kākāpō breeding is tightly tied to rimu mast years. [[7]](cite://7/1) Radio telemetry and, more recently, transmitters worn by every single bird allow continuous tracking. [[8]](cite://8/1)

Supplementary feeding has also been a key tool, with a nutritional cycle-based feeding strategy proving effective at triggering breeding events. [[9]](cite://9/1) The programme has grown the population from just 51 known birds in 1995 to 237 today. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Takahē: Captive Breeding, Predator Control, and Wild Reintroduction

The takahē programme has placed greater emphasis on captive breeding and wild reintroduction across multiple sites. In the early 1980s, eggs were incubated and chicks raised in enclosures near Te Anau. [[10]](cite://10/1) The Burwood Bush Rearing Unit became the hub of this effort, producing approximately 25 chicks annually. [[11]](cite://11/1)

A critical and ongoing challenge for takahē — more so than for kākāpō on their island sanctuaries — is predator control on the mainland. Stoats are described as the takahē's greatest foe, and the programme has involved 1,600 traplines across 500 square kilometres of Fiordland terrain. [[12]](cite://12/1) After a 2007 beech-mast event triggered a stoat population explosion, the wild Murchison Mountains population declined from around 160 birds. [[13]](cite://13/1)

The takahē programme has also pursued a broader geographic spread, reintroducing birds to Kahurangi National Park in 2018, to Ngāi Tahu land at Greenstone Station in 2023, and to the Rees Valley in 2025 — establishing multiple wild populations. [[3]](cite://3/2) By 2023, the total population had reached 500 birds. [[3]](cite://3/3)

![embed-2](embed://2)

## A Shared Pivot: Stepping Back from Intensive Intervention

Interestingly, both programmes are now moving in the same direction — away from hyper-intensive management and towards greater self-sufficiency.

For takahē, DOC embarked on what was described as "the great takahē experiment" — leaving the Murchison Mountains population largely unmanaged to test whether it is self-sustaining, while establishing an insurance population elsewhere. [[14]](cite://14/1) The new hands-off approach means eggs in the Murchison Mountains are now left to incubate naturally rather than being collected. [[15]](cite://15/1) By 2024–25, the Murchison population had reached carrying capacity of an estimated 220–260 birds, and DOC felt confident enough to step back from rigorous monitoring there. [[16]](cite://16/1)

For kākāpō, the 2026 breeding season — the largest on record — has marked a similar turning point. DOC is now trialling a "lighter touch" approach on two of the three breeding islands, with fewer chick checks, more eggs hatching naturally in nests rather than in incubators, and a general move towards minimal intervention. [[8]](cite://8/3)[[17]](cite://17/1) The ultimate long-term vision is to restore kākāpō to forests as wild, unnamed birds — with the Predator Free Rakiura programme on Stewart Island seen as a potential pathway to achieving this. [[18]](cite://18/1)[[17]](cite://17/2)

Both programmes also share the challenge of dependency on sustained human effort. As one kākāpō conservationist put it, if the human support were withdrawn for financial, social, or political reasons, decades of good work could quickly be undone. [[19]](cite://19/1) The shared goal, for both species, is to eventually work themselves out of a job.

*The most recent material used in this answer is from May 2026.*

cases.prompt: Compare the conservation approaches for the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes.

response.response_text:
Both the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes share a foundation of intensive human intervention to pull critically endangered flightless birds back from the brink — but they differ significantly in their habitats, specific techniques, and the trajectories they are now taking. Both programmes are managed by the Department of Conservation (DOC) and represent some of New Zealand's most ambitious and resource-intensive conservation efforts.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## A Shared Starting Point: Intensive Intervention

Both species were in dire straits when their recovery programmes began in earnest. The kākāpō programme, which started in its current form in 1995 with just 51 known birds, involved relocating every known wild kākāpō to predator-free offshore islands to halt their decline [[1]](cite://1/1). Similarly, the takahē programme — launched after the species was rediscovered in the Murchison Mountains in 1948 — established the Burwood Takahē Centre in the 1980s for captive breeding and chick rearing, and set up "security populations" on predator-free offshore islands [[2]](cite://2/1)[[3]](cite://3/1).

Both programmes have relied heavily on:
- **Translocation** to predator-free island sanctuaries [[4]](cite://4/1)[[2]](cite://2/2)
- **Captive breeding** and egg incubation to reduce chick mortality [[3]](cite://3/2)[[1]](cite://1/2)
- **Radio telemetry and transmitters** on individual birds to track movements [[5]](cite://5/1)[[6]](cite://6/1)
- **Predator control** as a central pillar of protection [[7]](cite://7/1)[[6]](cite://6/2)

## Kākāpō: Technology-Driven, Island-Based Management

The kākāpō programme has been defined by its extraordinary level of individual monitoring and technological innovation. Today, all 235 adult kākāpō have names, detailed family trees, and high-tech transmitters logging their activity [[5]](cite://5/2). Breeding seasons trigger an intensive suite of interventions: artificial insemination, egg incubation, supplementary feeding tied to rimu mast cycles, and hand-rearing of struggling chicks [[1]](cite://1/3).

Nest minding — where volunteers spend weeks in the field providing round-the-clock surveillance of individual nests — became a hallmark of the programme [[8]](cite://8/1). Infrared cameras, electronic monitoring systems, and even a portable "boom box" to encourage male courtship behaviour were all developed specifically for kākāpō [[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1).

The programme has also grappled with the birds' unusual biology: kākāpō only breed every two to four years, triggered by rimu tree fruiting (mast) events, making each breeding season a high-stakes, carefully orchestrated effort [[1]](cite://1/4). German scientists collaborating with DOC have also found that artificial insemination significantly increases egg fertility rates [[11]](cite://11/1).

Currently, kākāpō breed on three remote islands, with a trial also underway at the fenced mainland sanctuary of Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari [[12]](cite://12/1)[[5]](cite://5/3).

## Takahē: From Captive Breeding Towards Wild Self-Sufficiency

![embed-2](embed://2)

The takahē programme has followed a somewhat different arc. After more than six decades of intensive intervention — including captive breeding at Burwood, egg collection from wild nests, and the introduction of juveniles to the Murchison Mountains — DOC embarked on a bold experiment: leaving the Murchison population largely unmanaged to test whether it could sustain itself [[13]](cite://13/1)[[14]](cite://14/1). The plan was to stop collecting eggs from wild birds and cease introducing new juveniles, while maintaining predator control, and simultaneously establish a second large insurance population [[14]](cite://14/2).

Predator control — particularly targeting stoats, described as the takahē's "greatest foe" — has become the programme's primary focus [[7]](cite://7/2)[[6]](cite://6/3). This has involved 1,600 traplines across 500 square kilometres of alpine habitat [[6]](cite://6/4). Wild birds have also been tracked down with the help of bloodhounds and relocated by air to establish new populations on offshore islands and in city sanctuaries such as Zealandia, Willowbank, and Orokonui [[7]](cite://7/3).

The takahē programme has also evolved its captive-rearing methods, moving away from puppet-rearing techniques towards natural parenting approaches at Burwood, producing around 25 chicks annually [[15]](cite://15/1). By 2023, the total population had reached 500 birds, and new wild populations have been established in Kahurangi National Park (2018), Greenstone Station in the Upper Whakatipu (2023), and the Rees Valley (2025) [[2]](cite://2/3).

## The Shared Shift: Stepping Back

Interestingly, both programmes are now moving in the same direction — away from intensive management and towards greater self-sufficiency for the birds.

For kākāpō, 2026 has seen the biggest breeding season on record, and for the first time in the programme's 31-year history, some new chicks are not being named — a symbolic step towards the ultimate vision of having kākāpō living as "nameless, wandering" wild birds in New Zealand's forests [[5]](cite://5/4)[[16]](cite://16/1). The programme is also trialling a "lighter touch" approach on two of the three breeding islands, with fewer chick checks and more eggs hatching naturally in nests rather than in incubators [[17]](cite://17/1).

For takahē, the Murchison Mountains population has reached carrying capacity — estimated at between 220 and 260 birds — and DOC has been able to step back from rigorous monitoring there, freeing up resources for new sites [[18]](cite://18/1). Despite more than three decades of effort, wild takahē numbers had not significantly increased for a long time, though with several small populations on predator-free islands, the species is no longer in danger of extinction [[19]](cite://19/1).

## Key Differences at a Glance

| Feature | Kākāpō | Takahē |
|---|---|---|
| Current population | ~235 adults (2026) | ~500 birds (2023) |
| Primary habitat | Predator-free offshore islands | Murchison Mountains + offshore islands + new mainland sites |
| Breeding trigger | Rimu mast events (every 2–4 years) | Annual |
| Key technology | Transmitters, infrared cameras, AI, GPS loggers | Radio telemetry, GPS, bloodhounds |
| Captive breeding | Hand-rearing, artificial insemination | Burwood Breeding Centre, natural parenting |
| Primary threat | Predators, low fertility, disease | Stoat predation |
| Current direction | Lighter-touch, moving towards wild future | Stepping back from Murchison, expanding to new wild sites |

[[5]](cite://5/5)[[2]](cite://2/4)[[18]](cite://18/2)[[17]](cite://17/2)[[6]](cite://6/5)[[1]](cite://1/5)

Both programmes stand as remarkable testaments to what sustained, science-led conservation can achieve — and both are now at an exciting inflection point, cautiously handing more of the future back to the birds themselves.

*The most recent material used in this answer is from May 2026. RNZ's most recent coverage in Tahi is from 12/05/2026.*

cases.prompt: Compare the conservation approaches for the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes.

response.response_text:
Both the kākāpō and takahē recovery programmes share a foundation of intensive human intervention to pull critically endangered flightless birds back from the brink — but they differ significantly in their habitats, specific methods, and the trajectories they are now taking. Both programmes are managed by the Department of Conservation (DOC) and both are now, after decades of hands-on management, beginning a careful shift toward less intensive approaches.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Shared Starting Point: Predator-Free Islands and Intensive Management

Both species were devastated by introduced mammalian predators — rats, stoats, ferrets and feral cats — and both programmes responded by relocating birds to predator-free offshore island sanctuaries. [[1]](cite://1/1)

For kākāpō, all surviving birds were uplifted from the mainland and transferred to predator-free islands including Whenua Hou/Codfish Island, Maud Island/Te Hoiere, and Little Barrier Island/Hauturu between 1982 and 1992. [[2]](cite://2/1) The kākāpō programme became famous for its extraordinary level of hands-on intervention: 24-hour volunteer nest minding, infrared surveillance cameras at every nest, nightly chick weighing, heat pads for struggling chicks, and hand-rearing. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1) Technical innovation has been a hallmark of the programme, with scientist Graeme Elliott developing devices such as a portable "boom box" to encourage male courtship calls, and experimenting with hormone injections in rimu trees to stimulate fruiting. [[5]](cite://5/1)

For takahē, intensive management similarly began in earnest in the 1980s, with the Burwood Takahē Centre established near Te Anau to manage captive breeding and chick rearing. [[6]](cite://6/1) Eggs were incubated and chicks raised in predator-proof enclosures, typically housing just two adults and two chicks per pen. [[7]](cite://7/1)[[8]](cite://8/1) Security populations were established on predator-free offshore islands as insurance against the loss of the wild Murchison Mountains population. [[6]](cite://6/2)

## Key Differences in Method

While both programmes use island sanctuaries and predator control, the specific challenges — and therefore the tools — differ considerably.

**Kākāpō** breeding is tied to the rimu tree masting cycle, meaning the birds only breed every two to four years when rimu fruit is abundant. [[2]](cite://2/2) This has led to a highly specialised supplementary feeding programme designed around nutritional cycles to trigger breeding. [[9]](cite://9/1) The programme also employs artificial insemination, genetic management to address severe inbreeding (around 40 percent of eggs are infertile due to a population bottleneck in the early 1990s), and genome sequencing of every individual bird. [[10]](cite://10/1)[[11]](cite://11/1) Every kākāpō has a name, a transmitter, and a detailed family tree. [[11]](cite://11/2)

**Takahē** face a different primary threat: stoat predation, particularly during beech mast years when stoat populations explode. [[12]](cite://12/1) The programme has maintained 1,600 traplines across 500 square kilometres of alpine habitat in the Murchison Mountains. [[12]](cite://12/2) Wild birds are tracked down with the help of bloodhounds and relocated by helicopter to establish new populations on offshore islands and in city sanctuaries such as Zealandia, Willowbank, and Orokonui. [[13]](cite://13/1) Unlike kākāpō, takahē have been successfully reintroduced to multiple mainland wild sites, including Kahurangi National Park (2018) and the Upper Whakatipu region (2023–2025). [[6]](cite://6/3)

![embed-2](embed://2)

## Population Outcomes

The two programmes have followed different trajectories. The kākāpō population grew from just 51 birds in 1995 to 237 adults by late 2025, with 2026 shaping up as the biggest breeding season on record — potentially pushing the population past 300. [[2]](cite://2/3)[[11]](cite://11/3) Despite this, the fertility rate remains only around 50 percent, and disease (such as the 2019 aspergillosis outbreak that killed nine birds) remains a constant threat. [[11]](cite://11/4)[[14]](cite://14/1)

Takahē have fared somewhat differently. Despite more than three decades of intensive effort, wild numbers did not significantly increase for a long time, though offshore island populations prevented extinction. [[15]](cite://15/1) However, the population reached an estimated 500 birds by 2023, and the Murchison Mountains population has now reached carrying capacity — estimated at between 220 and 260 birds — allowing DOC to begin stepping back from active monitoring there. [[6]](cite://6/4)[[16]](cite://16/1)

## The Shared Future: Stepping Back

Both programmes are now navigating the same philosophical shift — from intensive intervention toward minimal management — though they are at different stages.

For kākāpō, the 2026 breeding season marks the first time a "lighter touch" approach is being trialled on two of the three breeding islands, with fewer chick checks, more eggs hatching naturally, and hands-off breeding sites established at Te Kākahu o Tamatea/Chalky Island in Fiordland. [[14]](cite://14/2)[[2]](cite://2/4) The ultimate vision, as expressed by operations manager Deirdre Vercoe, is to have kākāpō "nameless, wandering through our forests, booming from the mountains." [[11]](cite://11/5) The programme is also investigating fenced mainland sanctuaries and watching the Predator Free Rakiura initiative with great interest. [[17]](cite://17/1)

For takahē, DOC has already begun leaving the Murchison Mountains population largely unmanaged to test self-sustainability, while establishing insurance populations elsewhere. [[18]](cite://18/1) The new hands-off approach means eggs in the Murchison Mountains are now left to incubate naturally rather than being collected. [[19]](cite://19/1) The takahē recovery team has described reaching carrying capacity in the Murchisons as "a big tick in the success box," freeing up resources for new sites. [[16]](cite://16/2)

Both programmes reflect a broader truth in New Zealand conservation: intensive human intervention has been essential to prevent extinction, but the long-term goal is always to restore these taonga species to a genuinely wild existence — and both are now, cautiously, beginning that journey.

*The most recent material used in this answer is from RNZ, dated 12/05/2026.*

# New Zealand's Economy: The Latest Picture

New Zealand's economy has been on a recovery path after a difficult few years, with the most recent data pointing to continued — if uneven — growth. Here is a summary of where things stand.

## GDP: Growth Returning

The most recent GDP figures in the search results come from June 2026, when Stats NZ reported that gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.8 percent in the three months to March 2026, with ANZ chief economist Sharon Zollner discussing the figures with RNZ. [[1]](cite://1/1)

Before that, the economy posted a strong rebound in the September quarter of 2025, with GDP rising 1.1 percent — well above expectations of around 0.9 percent — to sit 1.4 percent higher than a year earlier. [[2]](cite://2/1)[[3]](cite://3/1) Growth was broad-based, with increases across 14 out of 16 industries, led by manufacturing and business services (both up 2.2 percent) and construction (up 1.7 percent). [[2]](cite://2/2) Exports rose 3.3 percent on the back of strong dairy and meat performances. [[2]](cite://2/3)

Earlier in 2025, GDP had grown 0.8 percent in the March quarter, driven by agriculture, manufacturing, and business services, though momentum appeared to slow in subsequent months. [[4]](cite://4/1)

Finance Minister Nicola Willis described the September 2025 result as evidence the economy was "getting back on track," saying growth in job-rich sectors like manufacturing and construction would lead to job creation and higher wages. [[2]](cite://2/4) Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds pushed back, arguing that over the full year ended September 2025, GDP had actually fallen 0.5 percent compared to the year prior. [[2]](cite://2/5) Willis countered that the economy was 1.3 percent bigger in the September 2025 quarter compared with the same quarter in 2024. [[2]](cite://2/6)

## The Westpac Outlook: Firmer Footing in 2026

In February 2026, Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold offered an optimistic assessment, saying New Zealand looked to be "on much firmer footing" after a rocky few years. [[5]](cite://5/1) Westpac estimated annual economic growth had lifted to 1.8 percent in the year ended 2025, with growth forecast to accelerate to 3.3 percent in 2026 and 2.7 percent in 2027. [[5]](cite://5/2)

Eckhold noted that average borrowing costs were expected to continue declining as more mortgage holders rolled off earlier fixed terms onto lower rates, supporting domestic demand. [[5]](cite://5/3) However, he cautioned that inflation — which had surprised to the upside at 3.1 percent in late 2025 — was projected to moderate only gradually, with core inflation likely to remain above the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's (RBNZ) 2 percent target midpoint through the rest of 2026. [[5]](cite://5/4)

## The Middle East Conflict: A Complicating Factor

A significant cloud over the outlook has been the conflict in the Middle East. A March 2026 GDP report noted that while the December 2025 quarter figures showed GDP rising 0.3 percent — below the Reserve Bank's forecast of 0.5 percent — economists considered those numbers largely overtaken by events, given the risks posed by oil price surges, inflation pressures, and supply chain disruptions stemming from the conflict. [[6]](cite://6/1) Treasury forecast inflation could reach 3.7 percent if the conflict persisted. [[6]](cite://6/2)

## Labour Market: Still Catching Up

The jobs market has lagged the broader economic recovery. As of August 2026, economists were warning that unemployment was set to push up to a near 11-year high of around 5.4 to 5.5 percent for the three months ended June 2026, with economic activity slowed by the US-Iran war and firms not actively hiring despite population growth. [[7]](cite://7/1) Wage growth was expected to remain subdued at around 2 percent. [[7]](cite://7/2)

Earlier, in February 2026, most major bank economists expected unemployment to linger around 5.3 percent for the December 2025 quarter, with only tentative signs that the labour market downturn had ended. [[8]](cite://8/1) The RBNZ was expected to hold the official cash rate (OCR) steady at 3.25 percent for much of 2026. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Regional Picture

Canterbury led New Zealand's regional economic rankings in ASB's March 2026 scoreboard, driven by strong dairy incomes, employment growth, retail spending, and tourism recovery. Otago and Waikato tied for second, while Auckland jumped from seventh to fourth. Wellington ranked last, hampered by weakness in housing, construction, and discretionary spending. [[9]](cite://9/1)

## Pre-Election Economic Update

In late September 2026, Treasury released its Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, prompting analysis from NZ Herald political editor Thomas Coughlan on where the economy is headed — though the detailed findings of that update are not fully captured in the available search results. [[10]](cite://10/1)

---

RNZ's most recent coverage in Tahi is from 29 September 2026. The situation — particularly around the labour market and the impact of the Middle East conflict — may have evolved since then.

# New Zealand's Economy: Latest Reporting

New Zealand's economy has been navigating a complex path — moving from recession and contraction through to tentative recovery, while now facing fresh headwinds from inflation pressures and global uncertainty. Here's a summary of the most recent reporting.

---

## The Most Recent Development: Reserve Bank Holds the OCR

The most up-to-date news in the search results concerns the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ), which shocked markets by holding its Official Cash Rate (OCR) unchanged at 2.75 percent in a split 4–3 decision. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1) Economists had universally forecast a 25 basis point rise, and were surprised by both the split vote and the dovish tone of the RBNZ's statement. [[1]](cite://1/2)

The decision was driven by mixed signals: fuel-price-driven inflation on one hand, and subdued household spending limiting firms' ability to pass on costs on the other. [[2]](cite://2/2) Annual inflation is expected to reach 4.4 percent in December, largely due to fuel price spikes. [[2]](cite://2/3)

ANZ chief economist Sharon Zollner called it "a close run thing," and said a December rate rise now looked the likely next step, with the OCR expected to rise to 3.5 percent with further hikes in February and March next year. [[1]](cite://1/3) ASB and Westpac economists also pencilled in a December rise, with financial markets pricing in a 75 percent chance of that outcome. [[1]](cite://1/4)

The New Zealand dollar fell close to a cent against the US dollar in the minutes following the announcement. [[1]](cite://1/5)

For home loan borrowers, economists are divided on what the hold means. Westpac's Kelly Eckhold noted the one-year swap rate had already dropped 20 basis points, suggesting possible mortgage rate decreases. [[3]](cite://3/1) However, Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub warned that any relief would be small, and that borrowers should prepare for the possibility of higher rates ahead. [[3]](cite://3/2)

---

## Pre-Election Economic and Fiscal Update

In late September 2026, Treasury released its Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, prompting wide discussion about where the New Zealand economy is headed. NZ Herald political editor Thomas Coughlan described it as a significant document attempting to answer what is going on with the economy and where it is heading. [[4]](cite://4/1)

---

## GDP: A Story of Recovery — With Caveats

New Zealand's GDP growth has been on a gradual upward trajectory after a difficult period:

- GDP rose **0.8 percent** in the three months to March 2026, according to Stats NZ figures. [[5]](cite://5/1)
- In the December 2025 quarter, GDP grew **0.3 percent**, below the Reserve Bank's forecast of 0.5 percent, with annual growth at 1.5 percent. [[6]](cite://6/1)
- The September 2025 quarter saw a strong rebound of **1.1 percent**, following a revised 1 percent contraction in the June 2025 quarter. [[7]](cite://7/1)

However, economists noted that the December quarter figures were rendered somewhat dated by the emergence of the Middle East conflict, which poses significant downside risks through oil price surges, inflation pressures, and supply chain disruptions. Treasury forecasts inflation could reach 3.7 percent if the conflict persists. [[6]](cite://6/2)

---

## The Broader Economic Picture

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said earlier in 2026 that the New Zealand economy looked to be "on much firmer footing," with annual growth estimated at 1.8 percent for 2025, accelerating to 3.3 percent in 2026 and 2.7 percent in 2027. [[8]](cite://8/1) The unemployment rate was expected to fall below 5 percent in the second half of 2026. [[8]](cite://8/2)

However, more recent reporting paints a more cautious picture. The RBNZ noted the economy had stalled in the second quarter of 2026, with households and businesses constrained by heightened global policy uncertainty, falling employment, higher prices for essentials, and declining house prices. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Finance Minister Nicola Willis has maintained an optimistic tone, saying the road to recovery "looked good" and urging New Zealanders to have confidence in the economy's future. [[9]](cite://9/2)

---

## Regional Snapshot

ASB's Regional Economic Scoreboard showed Canterbury leading New Zealand's regional growth for a third consecutive quarterly win in 2025, driven by strong dairy incomes, employment growth, retail spending, and tourism recovery. Otago and Waikato tied for second, while Auckland jumped from seventh to fourth. Wellington ranked last, hampered by weakness in housing, construction, and discretionary spending. [[10]](cite://10/1)

# New Zealand's Economy: Where Things Stand

The most recent reporting available points to an economy navigating a gradual recovery, with inflation re-emerging as a key concern heading into late 2026.

## Inflation Ticks Down — But Not for Long

The most up-to-date data comes from an RNZ report published on 22 October 2026, covering the September quarter inflation figures. New Zealand's inflation rate eased to 3.7 percent in the September quarter, down from 4.1 percent in June, driven largely by a temporary dip in fuel prices — petrol fell 6.5 percent due to improved global supplies. [[1]](cite://1/1)

However, that relief is expected to be short-lived. Underlying inflation measures point to an annual rate of between 2.6 and 3.2 percent, and the September quarter's reprieve has already begun to evaporate as global fuel costs have surged again, sending local pump prices to record highs. [[1]](cite://1/2) Inflation is now expected to climb as high as 4.5 percent in the December quarter, raising the prospect of spillover into other goods and services and stronger wage demands. [[1]](cite://1/3)

Financial markets are currently pricing in a 25 basis point Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) rate rise on 28 October, with a 50 percent chance of a further rise in December. [[1]](cite://1/4)

## Treasury's Pre-Election Update

In late September 2026, Treasury released its Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (Prefu), offering a comprehensive look at the medium-term outlook. The headline finding: New Zealand's recovery has been delayed by the Middle East conflict, but not derailed. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Key forecasts from the Prefu include:

- Annual average growth is projected to peak at 3 percent by March 2028, slightly down from the 3.2 percent forecast in May's Budget. [[2]](cite://2/2)
- Unemployment is forecast to fall from 5.6 percent to 4.3 percent by 2030. [[2]](cite://2/3)
- Inflation is expected to decline to just below 2 percent in 2027. [[2]](cite://2/4)
- Housing price growth has been revised sharply downward — just 0.6 percent growth forecast for 2027, compared with 4 percent in the Budget, attributed to higher interest rates, increased housing supply, and lower net migration. [[2]](cite://2/5)

Treasury flagged that its forecasts were issued in mid-August and may not fully account for the more recent surge in crude oil prices and spikes in global government borrowing costs. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## The Recovery Picture: Cautious Optimism

Earlier in 2026, several bank economists had been cautiously optimistic. ASB's chief economist Nick Tuffley said in July that the economy had "shown greater resilience than many expected" in the face of global uncertainty and higher fuel prices. [[4]](cite://4/1) GDP grew 0.8 percent in the March quarter, and Tuffley said the recovery appeared to be back on track, supported by resilient commodity prices, recovering tourism (at 93 percent of pre-Covid visitor levels), and easing fuel costs at the time. [[4]](cite://4/2)

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan, also writing in July, forecast economic growth reaching a four-year high of 2.7 percent in mid-2027, though he cautioned that recovery remained "at the mercy of the geopolitical situation overseas." [[5]](cite://5/1) He expected the official cash rate (OCR) to reach 3.0 percent by year-end and 3.5 percent in 2027 — driven by improving economic conditions rather than inflation-fighting. [[5]](cite://5/2)

## Regional Picture

Canterbury has been leading New Zealand's regional growth, recording its third quarterly win in ASB's Regional Economic Scoreboard in early 2026, driven by strong dairy incomes, employment growth, retail spending, and tourism recovery. Auckland rebounded from seventh to fourth place, while Wellington ranked last, hampered by weakness in housing, construction, and discretionary spending. [[6]](cite://6/1)

## The Risks Ahead

The key risks to the outlook are consistent across forecasters:

- Ongoing Middle East conflict and elevated energy prices pushing inflation higher for longer. [[1]](cite://1/5)[[2]](cite://2/6)
- Slower-than-expected recovery in China, New Zealand's largest trading partner, dampening agricultural demand. [[7]](cite://7/1)
- Global trade tensions and potential new tariffs weakening export performance. [[7]](cite://7/2)
- Domestically, persistent labour shortages and wage pressures could restrain productivity. [[7]](cite://7/3)

Tahi's most recent coverage on this topic is from 22/10/2026. Given the fast-moving nature of inflation and interest rate decisions, the situation may have developed further since then.

Ko te tikanga o **kaitiakitanga** ko te tiaki, te manaaki, me te ārai i te taiao — ā, ko tōna reo Pākehā ko *guardianship* me *protection*. [[1]](cite://1/1)

He ara whakahaere taiao tēnei, i ahu mai i te ao Māori, i te whakaaro ko ngā tāngata he wāhanga o te taiao, kāore he mea motuhake. [[2]](cite://2/1) Ko te kupu *tiaki* te pūtake o tēnei kupu — ko tōna tikanga ko te tiaki, te tohu, te ārai, me te manaaki. Nō reira, ko ngā whakaaro o te tiakitanga me te ārai kei roto i te ngākau o kaitiakitanga. [[3]](cite://3/1)

Ko te **kaitiaki** he tangata, he rōpū rānei e mōhiotia ana hei kaitiaki e ngā tangata whenua o tētahi rohe — hei tiaki i tētahi roto, ngahere rānei. [[4]](cite://4/1) I te ao Māori, ko ngā atua o te taiao ngā kaitiaki tuatahi — ko Tāne, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Ko ērā atu kaitiaki katoa e whai ana i ērā tūāhuatanga. [[5]](cite://5/1)

E kore e mutu, ka taea hoki te kaitiakitanga ki ngā taonga tuku iho — pērā i ngā korowai, ngā mere pounamu, me ngā pukapuka whakapapa. Ka tiakina ēnei taonga e tētahi kaitiaki mō te katoa o ngā uri. [[6]](cite://6/1)

I tēnei rā, kua whakaurua te kaitiakitanga ki ētahi ture, pērā i te Resource Management Act 1991, e kī ana ko kaitiakitanga "the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources." [[7]](cite://7/1)

Ko te pūtake o te kupu ko **tiaki**, e mārama ana ko "to guard" — ā, ko ōna tikanga anō ko "to preserve, foster, protect and shelter." Nō reira, ko ngā ariā o te tiaki me te ārai kei te ngākau o tēnei kupu. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Ko te **kaitiaki** he tangata, he rōpū rānei e manaakitia ana e te tangata whenua hei tiaki mō tētahi wāhi — pērā i tētahi roto, ngahere rānei. [[3]](cite://3/1) Ko te kupu **kai** he tohu mō tētahi e mahi ana i tētahi mahi, nō reira ko te kaitiaki he "carer, guardian, protector and conserver." I whakaarohia ngā atua o te ao tūroa ko rātou ngā kaitiaki tuatahi — ko Tāne, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. [[4]](cite://4/1)

E hāngai ana tēnei ariā ki te whakaaro Māori, ko ngā tāngata he wāhanga o te ao tūroa, kaua ko ērā e noho motuhake ana. [[5]](cite://5/1) Nō reira, he mea nui ake ake tēnei i te "resource management" noa iho — he **reverence** (whakaaro nui) ki te ao, me te pupuri i tōna mauri. [[6]](cite://6/1)

cases.prompt: Give me a comprehensive overview of the history of New Zealand's national parks.

response.response_text:
# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks represent one of the country's most treasured legacies — a network of protected landscapes stretching from volcanic plateaus to ancient rainforests, fiords, and glaciers. As of 2021, New Zealand has 13 national parks, each preserving scenery, ecological systems, or natural features considered so significant that their permanent protection is in the national interest. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Origins: Why National Parks Were Created

The push to protect New Zealand's wild places grew from several converging concerns in the late 19th century. Some settlers were alarmed that clearing forests for farmland was destroying spectacular scenery. A handful of scientists worried about the loss of native plants and wildlife, particularly birds. And the government was increasingly aware of the tourism potential of New Zealand's extraordinary natural landscapes. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Growing support for national parks among some Pākehā, combined with the desire of Māori to protect their ancestral lands, provided the essential context for the creation of the country's first national park. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## Tongariro: The First National Park (1887–1894)

The story of New Zealand's first national park is inseparable from the vision and mana of Ngāti Tūwharetoa. In the 1880s, ownership of the central North Island volcanoes was being disputed in the Māori Land Court, and there was a real danger that the peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe, and Tongariro would be divided and sold. [[4]](cite://4/1)

Horonuku Te Heuheu, paramount chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, expressed the stakes clearly: "Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro." [[4]](cite://4/2) In 1887, on the advice of his son-in-law, the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace, Horonuku signed a deed with the Crown ensuring the mountain block could never be sold. [[5]](cite://5/1) The government subsequently purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by an 1894 act of Parliament. [[4]](cite://4/3)

Tongariro remains New Zealand's most visited national park and is today a dual World Heritage Site, recognised for both its cultural and natural significance. [[6]](cite://6/1) In 2019 its total area was 78,618 hectares. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## Early Expansion: Parks Before 1952

Following Tongariro, the national parks network grew steadily. By 1900, parks had been created at Taranaki (Mt Egmont) — designated New Zealand's second national park — and large areas of South Island mountain lands had been set aside at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur's Pass. [[8]](cite://8/1) Almost a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland in 1905. [[8]](cite://8/2)

Abel Tasman National Park was created in 1942 to mark the tercentenary of Abel Tasman's arrival in New Zealand, largely through the advocacy of Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Parallel to the parks movement, conservationist Harry Ell championed the Scenery Preservation Act of 1903, which established a commission to investigate areas suitable for preservation. By the time Ell left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created nationwide — many of which, such as those at Aoraki/Mt Cook and in the Paparoa Range, later formed the basis of future national parks. [[10]](cite://10/1)

Until the 1940s, New Zealand's national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism, following the American model that prioritised visitor pleasure over nature conservation. [[11]](cite://11/1)[[12]](cite://12/1)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A Turning Point

In the 1940s, organisations such as the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs argued for centralised control of the parks. This movement led directly to the National Parks Act 1952, which established the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy. Individual park boards worked alongside the Department of Lands and Survey, which managed day-to-day operations through a park ranger service. Crucially, the Act emphasised that native plants and animals would be preserved, and introduced species controlled or exterminated. [[13]](cite://13/1)

The 1950s and 1960s became a golden age for the parks. The number of national parks quickly grew from four to ten within a few years of the Act's passing. [[14]](cite://14/1) The New Zealand Forest Service entered the picture in 1954 with the first State Forest Park — Tararua — offering an alternative model of protected land management. [[14]](cite://14/2)[[15]](cite://15/1)

During these years, the government embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track cutting, and footbridge construction. In 1960 alone, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut a week. Between 1957 and 1972, it completed 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[14]](cite://14/3)

## Wilderness Areas: Protecting the Wildest Places

As access to the backcountry improved, conservationists began calling for restraint — warning that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being tamed by overdevelopment. The answer was the creation of designated Wilderness Areas: places free of huts, tracks, bridges, and even helicopter access. [[14]](cite://14/4)

The first wilderness area, Otehake (12,000 hectares) in Arthur's Pass National Park, was established in 1955. [[16]](cite://16/1) In 1974, the first large wilderness areas — Pembroke, near Milford Sound, and Glaisnock (the country's biggest at 125,000 hectares) — were created in Fiordland National Park. [[17]](cite://17/1)

The country's first wilderness conference was held at Rotoiti Lodge in Nelson Lakes National Park in 1981. At that time there were seven wilderness areas, all within national parks. [[17]](cite://17/2) From 1988, wilderness areas were also created outside the national park system, including the 87,000-hectare Tasman Wilderness Area. [[18]](cite://18/1) By 2006, New Zealand had 11 wilderness areas in total. [[18]](cite://18/2)

## Legislative Reform and the Department of Conservation

The National Parks Act 1980 addressed growing scientific and conservation concerns by adding ecological systems to the list of features meriting national park status, and allowing for "specially protected areas" within parks. [[19]](cite://19/1)

In 1987, the act establishing the Department of Conservation (DOC) referenced the Treaty of Waitangi for the first time. After 1987, Treaty principles were applied to earlier laws covering parks and reserves, leading to significantly more consultation with iwi. [[19]](cite://19/2) In 1990, the National Parks Authority and park boards were abolished, replaced by the New Zealand Conservation Authority and local conservation boards. [[20]](cite://20/1) The public's right of access to national parks was to be balanced with the need to protect plants, animals, and natural features, with restrictions placed on buildings, roads, vehicles, and aircraft. [[21]](cite://21/1)

## Kahurangi and Later Parks

New parks continued to be added in the latter decades of the 20th century. Kahurangi National Park — New Zealand's 13th national park, established in 1995 — preserves one of the country's largest wilderness tracts in north-west Nelson. Its path to protection was long and contested, with mining and forestry interests competing against conservation advocates for decades. [[9]](cite://9/2)[[22]](cite://22/1) As one advocate noted, "If north west Nelson had been Sir Edmund Hillary's stomping ground, it would probably have been a national park years ago." [[9]](cite://9/3)

## Māori Perspectives and Te Urewera

A critical thread running through the history of New Zealand's national parks is the evolving recognition of Māori perspectives. Western concepts of "wilderness" often rendered Indigenous homes and relationships with the land invisible. The 2014 settlement with Tūhoe over Te Urewera represented a transformative shift: the land was recognised as a legal entity with its own mana and mauri, with Tūhoe as guardians and governors — a model that challenges and enriches the conventional national parks framework. [[16]](cite://16/2)

New Zealand's national parks today offer what has been called a "Recreation Opportunity Spectrum" — choices for experiencing the backcountry tailored to every need and ability, from fully formed paths to unmarked mountain routes. [[14]](cite://14/5) They remain, as botanist Leonard Cockayne once envisioned, a "noble recreation ground, great laboratory and training school" — and, given increasingly urban lives, more necessary than ever. [[14]](cite://14/6)

cases.prompt: Give me a comprehensive overview of the history of New Zealand's national parks.

response.response_text:
# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks represent one of the country's most treasured legacies — a story stretching from an extraordinary act of Māori generosity in 1887 through to ongoing debates about conservation, access, and Treaty obligations today. As of 2021, New Zealand has 13 national parks, protecting some of the country's most spectacular landscapes, from volcanic peaks to ancient glaciers and remote fiords. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Seeds of Conservation: Early Ideas and Advocacy

The intellectual groundwork for national parks was laid well before the first park was gazetted. Naturalist Thomas Potts was among the earliest voices, proposing in 1872 that Resolution Island become a reserve, and his 1878 article on "National Domains" marshalled the ideas that would precipitate the foundation of national parks from 1894. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Several motivations drove early conservation thinking in New Zealand. Some settlers were alarmed that clearing forests for farms was destroying scenic landscapes; a few scientists worried about the loss of native plants and wildlife; and the government was becoming aware of the tourism potential of the country's natural wonders. [[3]](cite://3/1) Premier Julius Vogel also championed conservation on utilitarian grounds — forests prevented soil erosion, provided sustainable timber, and shaped the "beauty, healthfulness and pleasure bestowing qualities" of the nation. [[4]](cite://4/1)

The Scenery Preservation Act of 1903, championed by politician Harry Ell, was a landmark moment. Ell argued passionately for setting aside reserves — "not merely for ourselves, but for the people who come after us." By the time he left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created, up from fewer than 100 when he entered. Many of these early reserves, such as those at Aoraki/Mount Cook and in the Paparoa Range, later formed the basis of future national parks. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## Tongariro: The First National Park

The founding of New Zealand's first national park is a story rooted in Māori land politics and cultural protection. In the 1880s, ownership of the central North Island volcanoes was being disputed, and Tūwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu feared the peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu would be divided and sold. He said: "Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro." [[6]](cite://6/1)

In 1887, on the advice of his son-in-law, the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace, Horonuku signed a deed with the Crown ensuring the mountain block could never be sold. [[7]](cite://7/1) The government purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by statute in 1894. [[6]](cite://6/2) It was both a convergence of growing Pākehā support for national parks and a Māori desire to protect ancestral land. [[8]](cite://8/1)

The Tourist Department developed the park as a visitor destination, but iwi involvement in park management was limited and diminished further after 1914 when the park was transferred from the founding trust board to the Tourist Department. Repeated requests for iwi recognition were refused for many years. [[9]](cite://9/1) A century later, in 1993, Tongariro became the first park in the world to receive joint World Heritage Status for both its landscape and cultural values. [[10]](cite://10/1)

## Early Expansion: 1900 to the 1940s

Following Tongariro, the network grew steadily. By 1900, national parks had been created on Taranaki (Mt Egmont) — designated the country's second national park — and large areas of South Island mountain lands had been set aside at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur's Pass. Almost a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland in 1905. [[11]](cite://11/1)

Until the 1940s, New Zealand's national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism, developed on the American model that prioritised visitor pleasure over nature conservation. [[12]](cite://12/1) This era saw grand gestures like the construction of the Chateau Tongariro hotel in 1929, and the Tourist Department taking over the resort in 1931 after its developer was bankrupted by the Depression. [[13]](cite://13/1) Abel Tasman National Park was created in 1942 to mark the tercentenary of Abel Tasman's discovery of New Zealand, championed by Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff. [[14]](cite://14/1)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A New Framework

In the 1940s, organisations such as the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs argued for central control of the parks. This movement led to the National Parks Act 1952, which established the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy. Boards oversaw individual parks in conjunction with the Department of Lands and Survey, which provided day-to-day management through a park ranger service. The Act emphasised that native plants and animals would be preserved, and introduced species controlled or exterminated. [[15]](cite://15/1)

The first four national parks had been created between 1887 and 1942, and six more were established between 1952 and 1964. [[16]](cite://16/1) The 1950s and 1960s became something of a golden age for outdoor recreation, with the number of parks quickly growing from four to ten. The government embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track cutting, and footbridge construction — in 1960 alone, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut a week. [[17]](cite://17/1)

Yet by the mid-1960s, there were still only 38 rangers managing over two million hectares of national park. Tracks were primitive and huts rare. [[16]](cite://16/2) Minister Ernest Corbett had added 1,200,000 acres to New Zealand's national parks during his tenure from 1949 to 1954, creating Urewera, Nelson Lakes, Tararua Forest and Mount Cook national parks, and establishing 147 scenic reserves. [[18]](cite://18/1)

## Modernisation: Bing Lucas and the 1970s Transformation

The most significant transformation of the modern national park system came under public servant Percy "Bing" Lucas, who was responsible for developing New Zealand's modern national park system from the early 1970s, balancing conservation and recreational values. [[19]](cite://19/1)

In 1969, Lucas was awarded a Winston Churchill Fellowship, enabling him to travel to the United States to study American national park management. He spent four months visiting Jasper, Banff, Mesa Verde and the Grand Canyon, and his subsequent report, *Conserving New Zealand's Heritage* (1970), became, in his words, "my bible for where New Zealand should go." [[20]](cite://20/1) He argued that parks should be preserved as natural environments, protected from commercial and industrial exploitation, while also catering to recreational users — best achieved through a well-funded, professional staff. [[20]](cite://20/2)

Under Lucas's direction, the ranger service was incorporated into the public service in 1969, creating uniformity of practice nationwide. Additional rangers were rapidly recruited, and from 1976 training was formalised through a specialised course at Lincoln University. Detailed plans for each park were developed, new visitor centres opened, and consistent high-quality signage was introduced. [[21]](cite://21/1)

## Legislative Milestones and the Department of Conservation

The National Parks Act 1980 addressed scientific and conservation concerns by adding ecological systems to the list of features meriting national park status, and allowed for "specially protected areas" within parks to guard against harmful human activity. [[22]](cite://22/1)

A major structural change came in 1987 when the fourth Labour government broke up the Department of Lands and Survey, moving its conservation functions — including management of national parks — into a new Department of Conservation (DOC). [[23]](cite://23/1) The 1987 Act that established DOC referenced the Treaty of Waitangi, and after 1987, Treaty principles were applied to earlier laws covering parks and reserves, leading to more consultation with iwi. [[22]](cite://22/2)

Kahurangi National Park, New Zealand's 13th, was established in 1995 after years of lobbying. Without a single influential advocate to push the issue, it had taken far longer than other parks to gain protection. [[14]](cite://14/2) Rakiura National Park on Stewart Island, created in 2002, is New Zealand's most recent national park, covering 157,000 hectares — about 85 percent of the island's land area. [[24]](cite://24/1)

## Māori Perspectives and Evolving Governance

The relationship between Māori and national parks has evolved considerably. The Western concept of "wilderness" has been challenged for rendering Indigenous homes invisible — many areas designated as wilderness were, in fact, ancestral homelands. response.response_text:
# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks represent one of the country's most enduring conservation achievements — a story stretching from an extraordinary act of Māori generosity in 1887 to a network of protected lands covering roughly one-third of the country today. It is a history shaped by indigenous values, settler ambition, scientific understanding, and an evolving sense of what wild places are truly worth.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The First National Park: A Gift from Ngāti Tūwharetoa

The origins of New Zealand's national park system are inseparable from the story of Ngāti Tūwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu Tukino IV and the sacred volcanoes of the central North Island. In the 1880s, ownership of the peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe and Tongariro was being disputed, and there was a real danger the mountains would be divided and sold. Horonuku understood what was at stake, saying: "Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro." [[1]](cite://1/1)

In 1887, on the advice of his son-in-law, the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace, Horonuku signed a deed with the Crown ensuring the mountain block could never be sold. [[2]](cite://2/1) The government subsequently purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by an 1894 act of Parliament — making it not only New Zealand's first national park, but one of the earliest in the world. [[1]](cite://1/2) At the time, the only other national park in existence was Yellowstone in the United States. [[3]](cite://3/1)

The park was initially developed by the Tourist Department as a visitor destination, but iwi involvement in management was limited and diminished further after 1914 when the park was transferred from the founding trust board to the Tourist Department. Repeated requests for iwi recognition were refused for many years. [[4]](cite://4/1)

## Early Motivations and the Second National Park

The push to create national parks in New Zealand was driven by several converging forces. Some settlers were concerned that clearing forests for farms was destroying scenic landscapes; a few scientists worried about the loss of native plants and wildlife; and the government was becoming aware of the tourism potential of New Zealand's natural wonders. [[5]](cite://5/1) Growing support among some Pākehā, combined with the desire of Māori to protect their land, provided the broader context for the national park movement. [[6]](cite://6/1)

Egmont National Park (now Taranaki/Egmont) became the country's second national park in 1900. The forest around the mountain had been protected by a reserve as early as 1875, after the provincial government recognised how rapidly bush in the district was being destroyed. The area within six miles (9.6 kilometres) of the summit was formally designated a national park in recognition of the splendour of its landscapes and forests. [[7]](cite://7/1)

Until the 1940s, New Zealand's national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism, rather than for conservation. [[8]](cite://8/1)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A New Framework

In the 1920s, boards were set up to manage Tongariro and Egmont national parks, but administrative and legislative arrangements across all parks remained uncoordinated. In the 1940s, groups such as the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs argued for central control. This movement led to the landmark National Parks Act 1952. [[9]](cite://9/1)

The new law established the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy. Boards oversaw individual parks in conjunction with the Department of Lands and Survey, which provided day-to-day management through a park ranger service. Crucially, the Act emphasised that native plants and animals would be preserved, and introduced species controlled or exterminated. [[9]](cite://9/2)

The 1950s and 1960s saw a rapid expansion of the system. The number of national parks quickly grew from four to 10 within a few years of the Act's passing. [[10]](cite://10/1) This was also a golden age for tramping, with the New Zealand Forest Service entering the picture in 1954 with the first State Forest Park at Tararua. Between 1957 and 1972, the Forest Service built 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[10]](cite://10/2)

## Wilderness Areas and Conservation Thinking

Such was the success of this infrastructure programme that purists began calling for restraint, warning that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being tamed by overdevelopment. The answer was the creation of designated Wilderness Areas — places free of huts and other amenities, without tracks, bridges, or even the possibility of a helicopter drop. [[10]](cite://10/3)

New Zealand's wilderness concept mirrored the United States' Wilderness Act of 1964, which dictated that wilderness land "shall be kept and maintained in a state of nature." The first wilderness area, Otehake (12,000 hectares) in Arthur's Pass National Park, was established in 1955. [[11]](cite://11/1) Progress was slow, and it was not until 1974 that the first large wilderness areas — Pembroke, near Milford Sound, and Glaisnock (the country's biggest at 125,000 hectares) — were created in Fiordland National Park. [[12]](cite://12/1)

By 1981, when the country's first wilderness conference was held at Rotoiti Lodge in Nelson Lakes National Park, there were seven wilderness areas, all within national parks. [[12]](cite://12/2) In 1988, the first wilderness areas outside the national park system were created, and by 2006 New Zealand had 11 wilderness areas in total. [[13]](cite://13/1)

## Law Changes and the Department of Conservation

The National Parks Act 1980 addressed growing scientific and conservation concerns. It added ecological systems to the list of features meriting national park status, and allowed for "specially protected areas" within parks to guard against harmful human activity. [[14]](cite://14/1)

A pivotal moment came in 1987, when the act establishing the Department of Conservation (DOC) was passed. Unlike the 1980 Act, this legislation did refer to the Treaty of Waitangi, and after 1987, Treaty principles were applied to earlier laws covering parks and reserves, leading to much greater consultation with iwi. [[14]](cite://14/2) In 1990, the National Parks Authority and park boards were abolished, replaced by the New Zealand Conservation Authority and local conservation boards. [[15]](cite://15/1)

## World Heritage Recognition and Māori Co-Governance

Several New Zealand national parks have been recognised as UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Westland Tai Poutini, Aoraki/Mount Cook and Fiordland national parks were listed in 1986, and in 1990, along with Mount Aspiring National Park, they were incorporated into a single vast site called Te Wāhipounamu South West New Zealand. Tongariro National Park was listed as a world heritage site for scientific reasons in 1990, and for its cultural significance in 1993 — the first in the world to receive dual status for both landscape and cultural values. [[16]](cite://16/1)

A transformative development came in 2014, when Te Urewera National Park was disestablished following a Treaty settlement with Tūhoe. The land was recognised as a legal entity with its own mana (authority) and mauri (life force), with Tūhoe as guardians and governors — a model that challenged Western concepts of conservation management and offered a new framework for incorporating indigenous worldviews. [[13]](cite://13/2)

## The Parks Today

New Zealand's most recently created national park is Rakiura National Park on Stewart Island/Rakiura, established in 2002. It covers 157,000 hectares — about 85 percent of the island's land area. [[17]](cite://17/1) DOC now administers New Zealand's largest recreation network, including more than 14,000 kilometres of tracks, 326 campsites, and approximately 950 backcountry huts across one-third of the country. [[18]](cite://18/1) Fiordland and Aoraki/Mount Cook are the two most popular national parks, and more than 50 percent of international visitors head to a national park during their time in New Zealand. [[19]](cite://19/1)

The history of New Zealand's national parks is, at its heart, a story about what a society chooses to protect — and for whom. From Horonuku Te Heuheu's extraordinary gift of sacred mountains to the ongoing evolution of co-governance with Māori, the parks reflect the country's deepest values about land, identity, and the future.

response.response_text:
# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks are among the country's most treasured taonga (treasures) — a network of protected landscapes stretching from the volcanic plateau of the central North Island to the remote fiords of the deep south. Their story is one of Māori generosity, settler conservation instincts, legislative milestones, and an evolving understanding of what it means to protect the natural world. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The First National Park: A Gift from Ngāti Tūwharetoa

The origins of New Zealand's national park system lie in an extraordinary act of rangatiratanga (chiefly authority) in 1887. Tūwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu was facing a real threat: different tribes were disputing ownership of the volcanic peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe and Tongariro, and there was a danger they would be divided and sold to Pākehā settlers. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Horonuku's response was to sign a deed with the Crown, ensuring the mountains could never be sold. As he put it: "Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro." [[3]](cite://3/1) The government subsequently purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by an 1894 act of Parliament — making it New Zealand's first national park, and one of the earliest in the world. [[2]](cite://2/2)

The park is today a dual World Heritage Site, recognised for both its cultural and natural significance. [[4]](cite://4/1)

## Early Expansion: The Turn of the 20th Century

The creation of Tongariro sparked momentum. By 1900, national parks had also been established on Taranaki (Mt Egmont) — the forest around the mountain had been protected by a reserve as early as 1875, with the area within six miles of the summit formally gazetted as the country's second national park in 1900. [[5]](cite://5/1) Large areas of South Island mountain lands were also set aside at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur's Pass, and almost a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland in 1905. [[5]](cite://5/2)

The motivations behind this early wave of protection were mixed. Some settlers were alarmed that clearing forest for farms was destroying scenic landscapes; a few scientists worried about the loss of native plants and wildlife; and the government was increasingly aware of the tourism potential of New Zealand's natural wonders. [[6]](cite://6/1)

Conservationist Harry Ell was a key figure of this era. His persistent advocacy in Parliament led to the Scenery Preservation Act of 1903, which established a commission to investigate which areas were suitable for preservation. By the time Ell left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created nationwide — many of which, such as those at Aoraki/Mt Cook and in the Paparoa Range, later formed the basis of future national parks. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## Tourism, Recreation and Early Management

Until the 1940s, New Zealand's national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism, following the American model that prioritised visitor pleasure over nature conservation. [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1) The Tourist Department developed Tongariro as a visitor destination, building huts at Ketetahi and Waihohonu by 1904, and in 1929 the grand Chateau Tongariro hotel opened on the slopes of Mt Ruapehu. [[10]](cite://10/1)[[9]](cite://9/2)

This era was not without controversy. For a decade from 1914, Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed in Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting — a move that drew sharp criticism from conservationists. [[9]](cite://9/3) Meanwhile, iwi involvement in park management was progressively diminished: after 1914, Tongariro was transferred from its founding trust board to the Tourist Department, and repeated requests for iwi recognition were refused for many years. [[11]](cite://11/1)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A New Framework

The post-war period brought a significant shift. Groups such as the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs argued for centralised control of the parks, and this movement culminated in the landmark National Parks Act 1952. [[12]](cite://12/1)

The new law established the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy, with boards overseeing individual parks alongside the Department of Lands and Survey. Crucially, the Act emphasised that native plants and animals would be preserved, and introduced species controlled or exterminated. [[12]](cite://12/2)

The 1950s and 1960s became something of a golden age for the parks. The number of national parks quickly grew from four to ten within a few years of the Act's passing. [[13]](cite://13/1) The New Zealand Forest Service entered the picture in 1954 with the first State Forest Park — Tararua — offering an alternative model of protected land management. [[13]](cite://13/2) The government also embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track cutting and footbridge construction: between 1957 and 1972, the Forest Service built 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[13]](cite://13/3)

## Wilderness Areas: Protection Within Protection

As access to the backcountry improved, conservationists began to worry that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being tamed by overdevelopment. The answer was the creation of designated Wilderness Areas — places free of huts, tracks, bridges, and even helicopter access. [[13]](cite://13/4)

The first wilderness area, Otehake (12,000 hectares) in Arthur's Pass National Park, was established in 1955. [[14]](cite://14/1) By 1974, the first large wilderness areas — Pembroke, near Milford Sound, and Glaisnock (125,000 hectares) — were created in Fiordland National Park. [[15]](cite://15/1) A national wilderness conference held at Rotoiti Lodge in Nelson Lakes National Park in 1981 helped formalise policy, at which point there were seven wilderness areas, all within national parks. [[15]](cite://15/2)

From 1988, wilderness areas were also created outside the national park system, including the 40,000-hectare Raukumara on the East Cape and the 87,000-hectare Tasman in what is now Kahurangi National Park. [[16]](cite://16/1) By 2006, New Zealand had 11 wilderness areas in total. [[16]](cite://16/2)

## Legislative Evolution and the Department of Conservation

The National Parks Act 1980 added ecological systems to the list of features meriting national park status, and allowed for "specially protected areas" within parks to guard against harmful human activity. [[17]](cite://17/1) Then in 1987, the Department of Conservation (DOC) was established, and its founding act referenced the Treaty of Waitangi — leading to greater consultation with iwi across all parks and reserves. [[17]](cite://17/2)

In 1990, the National Parks Authority and park boards were abolished, replaced by the New Zealand Conservation Authority and local conservation boards. [[18]](cite://18/1) These new bodies were made responsible for all conservation land, balancing public access with the need to protect plants, animals and natural features, and placing restrictions on buildings, roads, vehicles and aircraft. [[19]](cite://19/1)

## New Parks and Māori Recognition

The later decades of the 20th century saw further additions to the network. Kahurangi National Park — New Zealand's 13th national park — was established in 1995 after years of lobbying, having faced significant opposition from mining and development interests. [[20]](cite://20/1) Abel Tasman National Park had been created much earlier, in 1942, to mark the tercentenary of Abel Tasman's arrival in New Zealand, largely through the advocacy of Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff. [[20]](cite://20/2)

A landmark moment for Māori came in 2014, when Te Urewera National Park was disestablished and the land recognised as a legal entity in its own right — with mana (authority) and mauri (life force) — and Tūhoe confirmed as its guardians and governors. This represented a transformative model for incorporating Indigenous worldviews into New Zealand's conservation policy. [[21]](cite://21/1)

Today, New Zealand has 13 national parks, protecting some of the country's most spectacular landscapes — from the glaciers of Westland Tai Poutini and the limestone caves of Kahurangi to the volcanic peaks of Tongariro and the fiords of Fiordland. [[21]](cite://21/2)[[1]](cite://1/2) With 1.7 million overseas visitors recorded in 2017 alone, the parks remain central to both New Zealand's identity and its economy. [[21]](cite://21/3)

P01.expected_ttft_profile: Lowest TTFT. Baseline floor and the fast-path candidate.
P01.what_it_isolates: Pipeline floor: one clean fact, query is its own search term. Minimal topic generation, single/few-KB retrieval, trivial evaluation, short answer.

P02.what_it_isolates: Confirms the floor isn't a one-off — another self-contained fact (Te Ara / NZDB).

P03.expected_ttft_profile: Higher than baseline. Gap vs P01 ≈ the fan-out + multi-KB eval cost.
P03.what_it_isolates: Query that legitimately spans NZDB, Te Ara, RNZ (and NZGeo) — retrieval fan-out and per-KB evaluation. Where one KB left on LLM-as-Judge would gate the whole response.

P04.what_it_isolates: Broad topic → multiple search queries across many KBs; stresses topic-generation breadth and multi-KB evaluation together.

P05.expected_ttft_profile: Highest pre-answer TTFT. Heavy topic-gen + eval; synthesis starts late.
P05.what_it_isolates: Multiple search queries, wide retrieval across time, genuine synthesis across many chunks. The case where a stronger answer model might pay off.

P06.what_it_isolates: Multi-entity comparative reasoning; cross-source synthesis (NZGeo, RNZ, Te Ara).

P07.expected_ttft_profile: Moderate TTFT. Watch for extra latency from recency handling.
P07.what_it_isolates: Recency-weighted retrieval, runtime date injection, recency evaluation logic; RNZ-heavy.

P08.expected_ttft_profile: ≈ baseline if the multilingual path is efficient; materially higher flags te-reo overhead.
P08.what_it_isolates: Bilingual classification, te reo handling, and the multilingual reranker (Cohere 3.5) on non-English input.

P09.expected_ttft_profile: Very low TTFT if the classifier short-circuits cleanly. If high, the classifier itself is the bottleneck.
P09.what_it_isolates: Classifier-only path — should be classed beyond-scope and short-circuit WITHOUT retrieval / eval / full synthesis. Isolates classification latency from the retrieval pipeline.
